conversation.content:
Hello — I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Today we’re going to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS, a short questionnaire that simply helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Nothing you share will leave this room, and there are no right or wrong answers — just whatever is true for you. We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer. Ready to begin?

To start, how have you been able to enjoy things lately — even little moments of laughter or pleasure?

I still smile when I see my little guy grab my finger, but most things feel kind of dim, like the volume’s turned down on everything. Even the stuff I used to love—watching my shows, going for coffee—just feels… flat, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes a silly thing my husband says will make me chuckle, but it feels forced—like I’m going through the motions. The laughter fades fast and I’m right back to feeling blank.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk or meeting a friend for coffee—but when the time comes, I don’t really feel excited. I still go, and parts are okay, yet that eager, “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… like yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “I must be missing something basic—other moms seem to have this figured out.” I know logically babies just cry, but I still catch myself turning it inward, feeling I’m falling short somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly I’m okay, but a couple of times this week I’ll suddenly picture him not breathing in the crib, or worry that his cough means something awful—even though he’s perfectly fine. The fear bubbles up, and I have to check the monitor or peek in the bassinet before I can relax again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had that full-blown panic feeling—just those quick flashes of worry about the baby. They pass once I check on him, so I wouldn’t call it scared or panicky, more like a sudden “what if” that’s gone in a minute or two.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like this morning—he wouldn’t latch, the laundry was piled up, and I felt as if I was drowning in little jobs. For a few minutes it all seemed too much, but once he finally fed and burped, I could breathe again and chip away at the mess. So it comes and goes, but I mostly keep my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve still been able to sleep pretty well—once I finally get to bed. It’s just that sometimes, when my head hits the pillow, my mind keeps circling around the day and I have trouble drifting off. It’s not every night, maybe two or three times this week, and once I’m out I stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like there’s a little cloud following me around. It’s not constant; I can still smile at the baby or chat with my mom. But yeah, most days there’s at least a stretch where I just feel kind of down and heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when he wouldn’t nap and I felt like I was failing, and once when my partner asked how I was doing and the question just made me tear up. It’s not every day, but yeah, the tears sneak out when the stress piles up.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself—he needs me. Even on the weepy days, that idea has never crossed my mind.

You're navigating the tender early weeks of motherhood with evident love for your son, yet you've noticed a persistent heaviness that dims your usual joy. Moments of laughter feel fleeting, activities you once anticipated now seem flat, and a cloud of sadness visits most days. You're working so hard-getting out for walks, caring for your baby, managing the house-but still find yourself tearing up when things pile up or when well-meaning questions touch the tender spot inside. You reassure yourself that babies cry and routines take time, yet self-doubt creeps in, especially when sleep is briefly elusive.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only forced, fleeting laughter—clear reduction from her usual enjoyment, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient still participates but reports a clear reduction in anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame for routine infant issues, indicating occurrence "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports specific intrusive worries about infant safety that arise suddenly and require checking behavior, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily sadness "most days" but not constant, aligning with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 14 meets the threshold (≥14) indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Core symptoms map to <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<quote>no eager, can't-wait feeling</quote>), depressed mood most days (<quote>little cloud following me around</quote>), concentration on infant safety worries, sleep difficulty 2-3 nights/week, and self-reproach about parenting competence. Symptoms began after delivery and persist past two weeks, causing distress but without self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next week
2. Begin daily mood tracking and brief self-compassion exercises (e.g., 5-minute breathing or journaling)
3. Share results with your partner or trusted support person and identify specific help with night feeds or household tasks to improve sleep
4. Consider contacting Postpartum Support International warm-line for peer support and local resources
5. Maintain infant contact while scheduling follow-up EPDS in 2-3 weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit (non-diagnostic)

<sym>Reported symptoms</sym>
- Persistent low mood, described as a “little cloud” most days
- Markedly reduced pleasure/anticipation (“laughter feels forced,” “no eager feeling”)
- Episodic tearfulness (twice this week)
- Initial insomnia 2-3 nights/week, rumination-driven
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant safety (brief, self-limited)
- Self-blame and guilt about perceived maternal competence
- Episodic sense of being overwhelmed, especially when tasks accumulate

<med>Pattern consistent with</med> mild-moderate postpartum depressive symptoms, with secondary anxiety features.

Safety: Denies any self-harm ideation; no protective concerns identified.

Risk factors: Primiparous, sleep disruption, infant-care stressors, internalized performance expectations.

Plan: Continue monitoring with standardized tool (e.g., PHQ-9/EPDS) at next contact; consider formal evaluation if symptoms persist ≥2 weeks or worsen.
